questions.q: Maxwell predicted that the visible light we see is only part of a family of electromagnetic waves. Listed in order from shortest wavelength to longest wavelength, which sequence of regions is correct?
options: Radio waves, microwave radiation, infra-red radiation, visible light, ultraviolet rays, X-rays, gamma rays
Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet rays, visible light, infra-red radiation, microwave radiation, radio waves
Gamma rays, X-rays, infra-red radiation, visible light, ultraviolet rays, microwave radiation, radio waves
Radio waves, infra-red radiation, microwave radiation, visible light, ultraviolet rays, gamma rays, X-rays
questions.explanation: From shortest wavelength to longest the regions run gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet rays, visible light, infra-red radiation, microwave radiation and radio waves. The shorter the wavelength, the greater the energy each photon carries, so gamma rays are the most energetic and radio waves the least.

questions.q: Identify which regions of the electromagnetic spectrum are ionising.
options: Only gamma rays
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays
Infra-red, microwaves and radio waves
Visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are highly ionising and X-rays less so; ultraviolet light is also ionising, but visible light is not. Infra-red, microwaves and radio waves are non-ionising because they do not deliver enough energy to individual electrons to free them from their atoms.

questions.q: Explain why describing infra-red, microwave and radio radiation as 'non-ionising' does not mean these wavelengths are safe. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Non-ionising means the radiation does not deliver enough energy to individual electrons to allow them to escape their atoms, so it cannot ionise. However, at sufficient intensities these wavelengths can still cause burns through heating. For example, infra-red rays from a fire are extremely dangerous and are often the cause of death in bushfires, even though they cannot ionise.

criteria.descriptor: States non-ionising means the radiation cannot give an electron enough energy to escape its atom.
Explains that at sufficient intensity it can still cause damage by heating/burns.
Gives a valid example, e.g. infra-red from a fire causing burns.

questions.explanation: The distinction the marker wants is mechanism: ionisation versus heating. Non-ionising radiation is harmless only at low intensity; a high-intensity infra-red or microwave beam still burns.

questions.q: A spectroscope disperses light into its constituent wavelengths. By what mechanism does a prism do this, and how does a diffraction grating achieve the same result?
options: A prism reflects each wavelength by a different amount; a diffraction grating absorbs the unwanted wavelengths
A prism refracts different wavelengths by different amounts; a diffraction grating disperses light because the diffraction of light passing through its slits depends on wavelength
Both a prism and a diffraction grating disperse light purely by reflection from a ruled surface
A prism diffracts light through narrow slits; a diffraction grating refracts light through glass
questions.explanation: Light entering glass is refracted towards the normal, and because different wavelengths are refracted by different amounts the light is dispersed into its colours. A diffraction grating instead relies on the fact that light passing through its small slits diffracts by an amount that depends on the wavelength, again separating the colours.

questions.q: From memory, state the three findings Kirchhoff and Bunsen reported in 1859 about the conditions that produce a continuous, an absorption, and an emission spectrum, and what those lines reveal about an element.
keyPoints: A continuous colour spectrum is produced by glowing solids or dense gaseous bodies (a continuous black body spectrum).

If a gas exists between the light source and the spectroscope, light is absorbed from the continuous spectrum at wavelengths characteristic of the chemical components of the gas (an absorption spectrum).
A glowing gas produces bright lines on a dark background at wavelengths characteristic of its chemical components (an emission spectrum).
No two elements produced the same spectrum, but every atom of a particular element produced the same spectrum, making the spectroscope a tool for identifying elements.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three source conditions plus the unique-fingerprint result (no two elements share a spectrum), grade yourself Good or Easy. The fingerprint point is what makes spectroscopy able to identify elements in a distant star.

questions.q: An absorption spectrum is produced by shining light with a continuous spectrum from an incandescent bulb through a cool gas. What does the cool gas do to that light?
options: It adds bright emission lines at new wavelengths the source did not contain
It heats up and shifts every wavelength towards the red end of the spectrum
It absorbs certain wavelengths and re-emits them in all directions, so the light reaching the spectroscope is deficient in those wavelengths
It reflects all of the light back towards the source, leaving a dark spectrum
questions.explanation: The cool gas absorbs photons at its characteristic wavelengths and re-emits them in all directions, not just forward along the beam. Along the line of sight those wavelengths are therefore depleted, leaving dark absorption lines cut into the otherwise continuous spectrum.

questions.q: The kinetic energy of an electron accelerated by a voltage is given by Ek = qV, where q is the charge on the electron, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the energy of an electron accelerated by 100 kV in an X-ray tube.
questions.explanation: A direct application of Ek = qV with the electron charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. These high-energy electrons slam into the anode and decelerate, releasing energy as the very high-frequency, high-energy X-rays at the top of the electromagnetic spectrum.

questions.q: Maxwell's equations give the speed of electromagnetic waves as v = 1/√(μ₀ε₀). Using the permittivity of free space ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² s² kg⁻¹ m⁻³ and the permeability of free space μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ m kg C⁻², calculate this speed.
questions.explanation: The figure that falls out, 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, equals the measured speed of light. Maxwell noticed this match, which led him to propose that the light we see is an electromagnetic wave.

questions.q: In 1868 Joseph Norman Lockyer detected a Fraunhofer line in the solar spectrum that did not correspond with any known element on Earth. What did he conclude, and how was it later confirmed?
options: He concluded the spectroscope was faulty; the line was never explained
He predicted an as yet undiscovered element in the Sun, named it helium after the Greek helios, and William Ramsay confirmed this in 1895 by isolating helium in the laboratory
He concluded the line came from hydrogen, which William Ramsay later renamed helium in 1895
He predicted a new element and named it after himself; it was isolated on Earth the same year
questions.explanation: Lockyer predicted there must be an as-yet-undiscovered element in the Sun and named it helium after helios, the Greek for Sun. William Ramsay confirmed this in 1895 by isolating helium in the laboratory, decades after it was first read in a solar spectral line.

questions.q: A prism and a diffraction grating both spread white light into a spectrum, but the order of colours reverses. In a prism, violet is deviated the most. In a diffraction grating spectrum, which colour is deviated the most?
options: Violet, exactly as in a prism
Green, because it is the central colour
Red, the longest wavelength, is deviated the most
All colours are deviated equally by a grating
questions.explanation: In a prism, short-wavelength violet refracts the most and red the least. A diffraction grating reverses this: the longest wavelength, red, is diffracted to the largest angle and violet the least. That reversal is the discriminating fact when a question asks which device produced a spectrum.

questions.q: Compare the emission and absorption spectra of a given element, and explain how spectra are used to identify the elements present in a gas. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: An emission spectrum consists of bright coloured lines on an otherwise dark background. It is produced by a hot, low-density gas such as the gas in a discharge tube: the discharge excites the atoms' electrons to higher energy levels, and as they fall back they emit photons of specific energies, and therefore specific wavelengths, giving bright lines only at those wavelengths. An absorption spectrum consists of dark lines crossing an otherwise continuous, rainbow background. It is produced when light from a continuous source passes through a cooler gas, which absorbs photons at particular wavelengths and re-emits them in all directions, depleting those wavelengths from the line of sight. The crucial point of comparison is that, for a given element, the dark absorption lines occur at exactly the same wavelengths as the bright emission lines, because both arise from the same electron energy-level transitions in that element's atoms. Spectra identify elements because every element produces a unique set of spectral lines and every atom of an element produces the same set; by comparing the measured line wavelengths with known laboratory spectra, the matching pattern reveals which elements are present.

criteria.descriptor: Describes the emission spectrum (bright lines on dark background) with its source: hot low-density gas / discharge tube.
Describes the absorption spectrum (dark lines on a continuous background) with its source: continuous light through a cooler gas.
Explains emission via electrons falling between energy levels emitting photons of specific wavelengths.
Explains absorption via the cool gas absorbing and re-emitting in all directions, depleting those wavelengths.
States the key link: absorption and emission lines fall at identical wavelengths from the same electron transitions.
Concludes each element has a unique fingerprint, so matching line wavelengths identifies the elements present.

questions.explanation: The discriminator between a band-four and a band-six answer is the same-wavelength link and the unique-fingerprint conclusion, not just 'one is bright and one is dark'.
